clue.text: Article and pair of trailers for part of Lord of the Rings

definitions.text: part of Lord of the Rings

blocks.note: the definite article
a pair is two
read as things that tow, rather than film previews

explanation.surface: Someone describes a film's grammar and its two trailers when promoting a Tolkien adaptation.
explanation.walkthrough: Trailers sits naturally beside a film title, suggesting previews; here it is a jokey word for vehicles that tow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Two Towers is the second volume of Tolkien's trilogy, so it is one portion of the whole work.

clue.text: New mother squeezing last drop of babe's formula

indicators.note: the final drop of something is its very end, so only the closing letter is kept
a new version of a word has its letters made over into a different order
to squeeze something is to hold it tight within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the closing letter of babe

explanation.surface: A new mum holds the bottle of baby formula until the final drop is squeezed out.
explanation.walkthrough: Formula looks like baby milk, but it means a mathematical statement; the mother is rearranged around the single letter rather than kept intact.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics a theorem is a proven proposition, often stated as a formula or rule.

clue.text: Ancient fruit tree

blocks.note: first meaning: older, senior by age
second meaning: a shrub or small tree bearing dark berries

explanation.walkthrough: Ancient fruit tree reads as one old tree, but it splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: An elder is an older person and also the Sambucus tree whose berries make elderberry wine.

clue.text: Threadbare, as football team's second kit might be

definitions.text: as football team's second kit might be

blocks.note: first meaning: frayed and thin from long use

blocks.clueFragment: as football team's second kit might be
blocks.note: second meaning: a change strip is put on for games played away from home

explanation.walkthrough: A football club's second kit is its away strip, so it is the kit that gets worn away; the phrase also means rubbed thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Fabric that has been eroded by use is threadbare, and an away kit is literally put on for away fixtures.

clue.text: Occasionally trod on lost utensils

indicators.note: something done only occasionally happens every so often, so only every other letter counts

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters of these words

explanation.surface: Someone keeps treading on kitchen implements that have been mislaid on the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Utensils are implements for a task, the same broad class of objects as tools.

clue.text: Rolling Stones breaking up, mostly dreary news

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the word loses its final letter
something breaking up falls apart, letting its letters be rebuilt in another order

blocks.note: dreary without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A headline reports the depressing story that the Rolling Stones are splitting up.
explanation.walkthrough: The band name is a trap: a rolling stone is the proverbial person who never settles in one place.
explanation.definitionFit: From the proverb 'a rolling stone gathers no moss', rolling stones are people who drift without settling, i.e. wanderers.

clue.text: Live on border

blocks.note: re means on or concerning, as in a letter heading
a border is an edge or side

explanation.surface: Someone is described as living right on the frontier.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to dwell or have one's home there, a formal synonym of live.

clue.text: Rain and flood's inside London railway station

indicators.note: the inside of a word is what remains between its first and last letters

blocks.note: rain is falling water
the letters of flood between its outer pair

explanation.surface: Rain floods into a London terminus, a familiar commuter misery.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after flood is 'is' in the surface but a possessive in the wordplay: the inside of flood.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo is one of London's main railway terminals, south of the Thames.

clue.text: Followed single on the radio

indicators.note: what is on the radio is only heard, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a single person may be chaste, abstaining from sex

explanation.surface: A listener tracked a hit single as it played on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: Single looks like a record to suit the radio, but here it means unattached and so chaste.
explanation.definitionFit: To chase someone is to pursue them, so having followed is having chased.

clue.text: I wondered about cover to keep kippers warm

indicators.note: about suggests turning things around and around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone puzzles over how to stop smoked fish going cold.
explanation.walkthrough: Kippers are smoked herrings, but here they are people who kip, i.e. sleepers; kip is British slang for sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: An eiderdown is a thick quilt filled with down, a bed covering that keeps sleepers warm.

clue.text: Hit show's beginning, one starring Alan Alda

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of show
Alan Alda played Hawkeye in the TV series M*A*S*H

explanation.surface: A TV show gets off to a successful start with Alan Alda in the lead.
explanation.definitionFit: A smash is a huge success, a smash hit, so the noun hit means the same thing.

clue.text: Radius stupidly erased in studies again

indicators.note: doing something stupidly means doing it wrongly, so the letters end up in a muddled order

blocks.note: r is the standard symbol for radius
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student foolishly rubbed out the radius while going back over geometry work.
explanation.definitionFit: To reread a text is to go through it a second time, so studies again is rereads.

clue.text: Incessant advice to person with bad back dropping book?

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it fall away, so a letter is taken out

blocks.clueFragment: advice to person with bad back
blocks.note: someone with a bad back should not stoop so much
b is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A sufferer keeps getting the same advice about their back, and perhaps about lifting books.
explanation.walkthrough: The sensible advice 'bend less' loses its B to leave ENDLESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something endless goes on without stopping, which is what incessant means.

clue.text: Make a hash of meal, dish abandoned around noon

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so these words enclose the extra letter
abandoned can mean wild and uncontrolled, so the letters are let loose into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
n is the abbreviation for noon
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook ruins lunch, the dish left untouched at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: Hash looks like a culinary word in this kitchen scene, but make a hash of is an idiom for botching.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a hash of something is to bungle it, which is what mishandling a task amounts to.

clue.text: In supermarket with trolley perhaps squeaking

blocks.note: first meaning: buying groceries
second meaning: informing on someone to the police, slang

explanation.walkthrough: Squeaking seems to describe the trolley's wheels, but it is slang for informing, as is shopping someone, British slang for betraying them to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a supermarket with a trolley is going shopping, and both squeaking and shopping mean grassing someone up.

clue.text: Queen's Head pub's maid, terrible disappointment

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, the very first letter
something terrible is in a dreadful state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the opening letter of Queen
taken as written, with the s
taken as written

explanation.surface: The barmaid at a pub called the Queen's Head proves a great letdown.
explanation.walkthrough: The Queen's Head looks like a pub name; it is split to take the head of Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A damp squib is a firework that fails to go off, hence an event that disappoints expectations.

clue.text: The Police, or retro party album?

indicators.note: retro means looking backwards, so the pieces are read from the end

blocks.note: a do is a party
an LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a record is by the band The Police or is an old-fashioned party compilation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Police looks like the rock band, which fits the album; plod is British slang for the police, from Mr Plod in Noddy.
explanation.definitionFit: Plod is a mildly mocking British slang term for the police force collectively.

clue.text: Mum put on aircon, cooking pasta

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: ma is a familiar word for mother
these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mum switches on the air conditioning while she cooks a pasta supper.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaroni is a variety of pasta in short hollow tubes.

clue.text: Rumbling noise from motorway – I don't like that at first

blocks.note: boo is a cry of disapproval
M is the prefix for British motorways, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Someone hears a roar of traffic from the motorway and objects to it.
explanation.walkthrough: At first tells you to put the cry of disapproval before the motorway's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A boom is a deep resonant sound, such as thunder or a rumbling explosion.

clue.text: Censors line in live recordings

indicators.note: in means placed within, so one piece is set inside the others

blocks.note: to live is to be, to exist
l is the abbreviation for line
EPs are extended-play records

explanation.surface: A censor cuts a line out of live recordings.
explanation.walkthrough: Live looks like the adjective in live recordings, but it is the verb to be; EPs are extended-play records.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadcaster bleeps rude words by covering them with a tone, which is censoring them.

clue.text: Be foolishly inconsiderate, putting a match on litter?

indicators.note: in an across answer, putting one thing on another sets it after, so the match piece follows the litter

blocks.note: litter is untidy mess
taken as written
a bout is a boxing or wrestling match

explanation.surface: Someone thoughtlessly tosses a lit match onto rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Putting the match on the litter places it after MESS in the across answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To mess about is to behave in a silly way, and to mess someone about is to treat them inconsiderately.

clue.text: Foot in cast, shuffle and talk nonsense

indicators.note: the foot of a down word is its bottom, so the final letter alone is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of cast
to shuffle is to walk awkwardly, to waddle

explanation.surface: Someone with a foot in plaster shuffles about while talking rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: Foot in cast reads as a plaster cast, but it means the last letter of the word cast.
explanation.definitionFit: Twaddle is silly talk, and as a verb it means to speak foolishly or prattle.

clue.text: Something close to Cardigan Island

blocks.note: first meaning: a knitted pullover, similar to a cardigan
second meaning: the largest of the Channel Islands

explanation.walkthrough: Cardigan is also a Welsh town and Cardigan Island sits nearby, so the clue looks like geography; the capital C hides a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A jersey is a knitted top much like a cardigan, and Jersey is a Channel Island.

clue.text: Announce Swift show

blocks.note: first meaning: to put into words
second meaning: fast, as of a train or delivery
third meaning: to reveal

explanation.walkthrough: Swift looks like Taylor Swift announcing a concert; the three words are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Express is a verb for stating or showing something and an adjective for fast, non-stop services.

clue.text: Relative is excellent secretary

blocks.note: grand means splendid or excellent
a PA is a personal assistant

explanation.surface: Someone's relative proves to be a superb secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandpa is a grandfather, a family member and so a relative.

clue.text: Beef, good and mature

blocks.note: g is the abbreviation for good
ripe means fully developed

explanation.surface: A butcher praises a cut of beef that has been well aged.
explanation.walkthrough: Beef sounds like meat, as mature beef suggests; here it is slang for a complaint.
explanation.definitionFit: Beef and gripe are both informal words for a grievance or complaint.

clue.text: Part of elevated facade modified, like Florence Cathedral?

indicators.note: part of says the letters come from a run inside the words that follow
elevated means raised, and in a down answer raising the letters runs them bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: Part of a raised building front has been altered, perhaps on Florence's cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: Brunelleschi's famous dome tops Florence Cathedral; the question mark marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Florence Cathedral is crowned with a huge dome, so it is domed; the cathedral is one example.

clue.text: Criticise wrapping for T-shirts and underwear

indicators.note: a wrapping is what lies around the outside, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: to pan is to criticise harshly, as a reviewer does
the first and last letters of T-shirts

explanation.surface: Someone complains about the packaging on a set of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Pants are underpants in British English, not trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage pants are underpants, an item of underwear.

clue.text: Wearing appropriate outfit for March, perhaps

definitions.text: Wearing appropriate outfit for March, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: dressed suitably for a spring month

blocks.clueFragment: Wearing appropriate outfit for March, perhaps
blocks.note: setter's reading: dressed in military kit for a parade march

explanation.walkthrough: The capital M sends you to the month and its weather; a march is a military parade, for which soldiers dress in regulation clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers on a march wear regulation military dress, so they are dressed in uniform.

clue.text: Musical is so long, with a score that's below par

blocks.note: so long is a farewell
in golf a birdie is one stroke under par for a hole

explanation.surface: A musical closes early, its score judged substandard.
explanation.walkthrough: Score and below par suggest poor music, but they are golfing terms.
explanation.definitionFit: Bye Bye Birdie is a 1960 Broadway musical about a rock-and-roll star drafted into the army.
